critic:wiring-and-code.verdict:
O1 and O2 can both be built, wired and made code-sound. Every fix below is the same for both, but neither is ready as drawn. ERP's real tabs put the two M3 screws through solid case. One WAGO 221-412 is drawn for two poles. The cover's Heyco strain relief needs Heyco's pliers (UL 1598 5.2.1) and may not fit the 4.4 under the cover. The 'tie' that keeps 120 V apart has no anchor. The Ø16 plate opening, the ground path and the cord's polarity are still open.
O2's +12 is more than needed: with a strain relief in the cover, a centred cord needs a canopy of about 55 to 60.
The lane's 'can't keep it centred in 150 x 50' is true only for a strain relief in the cover. With the grip back in the canopy's floor (v8's flush gland), or no grip if the lab accepts 11.6.6, the centred cord needs about 7.5 above the cover. The real driver leaves 9.8, so a centred cord fits 150 x 50.

findings.claim:
The driver's fixing is drawn on a placeholder that is wrong in shape, place and thickness, so the two M3 screws that hold the driver and hang the enclosure go through solid case.
- ERP's ESS case has no end tabs. Its two mounting tabs are corner tabs inside the 84 x 40 outline, 1.8 thick. Their Ø3.2 holes are at diagonally opposite corners, 77 x 33 apart.
- The lane draws two 20 x 6 x 1 tabs on the centreline, 80 apart, which make the driver 86 long.
- At ERP's real holes, one SO-M3 standoff is 5.95 from a box-screw hole (PEM asks 6.0) and 1.5 from that screw's head. Moving the driver 1 to 2 along the enclosure clears it; each end gap is 7.
- ERP's leads leave at the base, which sits against the enclosure's top once the driver hangs base-up. They are drawn at mid-height.
With ERP's 1.8 tab, M3 x 6 still gets 3.2 of thread in the standoff.

One WAGO 221-412 is ordered and drawn for four conductors: the driver's red and black leads and the cord's two conductors.
- A 221-412 has two ports and joins them into one node, so it serves one pole.
- Four conductors will not go into one. If two pairs were forced into one node, the driver's output would be shorted.
- Two are needed. Both fit: 1.5 to spare under the real driver in O1, 13.5 in O2.
- The part suits 18 AWG stranded. WAGO's strip length is 11, and ERP's leads come stripped 9.5 and tinned, so re-strip them.

findings.claim:
The cover's straight-through strain relief cannot yet be fitted and pull-tested as drawn.
(a) Tool. The Heyco part for an SV/SVT 18/2 cord of 5.6-6.2 is SR 5MN-3 (#1157). It goes on with Heyco's squeeze pliers. A cord cut to length at installation cannot use it under UL 1598 5.2.1 unless the pliers ship with the lamp.
(b) Size. It is 11.1 overall (Heyco's C covers head and body), not the drawn 12.5. Heyco publishes no head thickness. Scaled from Heyco's own side view it is about 4.6 (UNVERIFIED). In both options only 3.4 is left between the cover and the floor grommet's 1.0 flange; the drawn head is 3.0, with 0.4 clear.
(c) Anchor. The 1.0 cover, held only by two M3 screws at its ends, cannot take UL's 156 N pull (17.21.1, at most 1.6 of movement). It would bend about 2.2 and yield. The test passes only if the relief bottoms on the floor grommet 0.4 below, so the canopy carries it.
Fix:
- a relief fitted with a screwdriver, such as a screw cord clamp inside, sized to the chosen cord's measured diameter (the cord row names no diameter);
- 5.5 to 6 under the cover, or a floor grommet without the inside flange;
- the relief near a screw, or a stiffer cover.
Heyco's tool-free snap-in cordgrips need 1.6-3.2 panels and are about 31 overall, so they do not fit.

UL 1598 6.17.2.2 accepts 'separate entries and reliable routing'. O1 and O2 now meet the first half: no field branch-circuit wiring enters the enclosure. 'Tie the leads to the input end' is not yet a reliable means.
- It exists only in the README. No tie, anchor, lance or clip is in the CAD, BOM or NOTES.
- It fixes only the 120 V side. The field-made Class 2 side is free to move: the cord's conductors, the splices, and the -XL driver's 300 mm output and dimming leads.
- As drawn the gaps are large: O1 26.8 to the Class 2 conductors and 51.1 to the splice; O2 37.7 and 57.2.
- In O1, though, the cord rises in the same 22 strip that carries the 120 V leads to the snap bushing, 26 along from it.
Fix, either:
- anchor the 120 V leads (a tie to a lance, or around the driver's case), fix the Class 2 splices in a carrier at the output end, and cut the output leads short at the factory; or
- a barrier (6.17.2.3/.4: at least 0.4 bonded steel or 0.7 fibre or rated polymer, gaps 1.6 at most). In O1 it runs across the strip, about 22 x 35.
In O2 the driver's body sits between the two sides, so a fixed splice place is probably enough. The lab decides (UNVERIFIED).

findings.claim:
UL 1598 11.5.3 is the clause that names this opening, not 11.4.4. By 11.5.3, both Ø16 and the old Ø22 fail.
- 11.4.4 limits luminaire mounting holes to 2.6 cm2 each. Ø16 (2.0 cm2) would pass it and Ø22 (3.8 cm2) would not, but this opening is a wiring passage, not a mounting hole.
- 11.4.1 puts any open hole within 13 of the mounting surface into four kinds. A wiring opening can only be an access opening.
- 11.5.3 asks for 'openings through a supporting strap, cross-bar, or plate': a single opening passing a 44.5 rod, or two of at least 10 cm2 passing a 16 rod.
- 11.5.1 lets a lamp of 4.54 kg or less be taken down for inspection 'without additional access openings'. The lab may read that as an exemption (UNVERIFIED).
It is safe either way to cut one Ø45 at (-11, 0), over the driver, with the steel top 4 below. It clears the SO-M4 by 9.3 to its edge (PEM asks 8), the box-screw holes by 21 and the gripper studs by 21, and lies inside a 4 in box.
The CAD cuts a plain Ø16, while the callout still says 'Ø22 ... rolled edge'. In 1.6 sheet, 5.14.1 asks only that the leads be kept off the edge: deburr or coin it, or bush it.

The green screw stays at (0, 56) on the plate, 1.25 past the enclosure's end.
- The supply's equipment grounding conductor must come down the Ø16 at (20, 26) beside the two leads, then run about 36 along the 4.0 gap over the enclosure's top.
- It passes about 3.9 from a box-screw head and 3.4 from ERP's real SO-M3. The snap bushing's head sits right under the opening.
- A bare 12 AWG fits. An insulated one (about 3.3-3.6, UNVERIFIED) has 0.4 to 0.7 left.
- It must be landed before the enclosure is hung. NOTES never say this, and still say 'the supply wired in it'.
Better: a factory green 18 AWG pigtail from that screw up through the opening into the box, spliced to the supply's grounding conductor with the supply. That puts the grounding means 'in the same location as the power supply connection' (6.14.2.2), and box fill omits it.
The enclosure's bond now rests on two serrated M4 screws (v9 had four). The two M3 heads bear on the driver's plastic tabs and do not bond. Two serrated screws should pass the bonding test (18.2), to be tested.

The cord is wired to the driver's red (+) and black (-) output leads at installation. UL 1598 5.2.7 requires 'matching identification' on conductors meant for field connection, and none is given.
- The cord row names a textile-braided 18/2 with no ribbed or coloured conductor.
- NOTES have no polarity step.
Name a cord with identified conductors, mark the driver's leads to match, and show it on the wiring diagram. Whether the ring board survives a reversed cord is UNVERIFIED; reverse-polarity protection on the board would make it moot.

findings.claim:
The lane's 'the cord can't stay centred in 150 x 50' is right only for a strain relief mounted in the cover.
If the grip moves back to the canopy's floor, the cover needs only a protected hole:
- the grip is a flush turned gland, like v8's 'turned 6061 gland ... its nut flush', worked from below once the canopy is up;
- the hole is a rolled edge, or a smooth hole in a cover of 1.1 or more.

The minimum canopy is then about 48 to 49:
3.0 floor + 4.4 under the cover + 1.0 cover + 7.4 + clearance + 25.2 driver + 1.0 top + 4.0 standoffs + 1.6 plate.
The splices go under the driver or in the strip.

Conditions:
- the floor grip is a made part that passes 156 N (17.21.1), with its inside part 3.4 or less, or the cover moves up within the 2.4 spare;
- the lab accepts it (UNVERIFIED);
- the owner accepts a flush ring the size of today's grommet.

critic:third-way.verdict:
Yes, a third way works in 150 x 50, and it beats both options. Stand the same ERP ESS010W-0180-42-XL on edge (40 tall, 25.2 wide) in a 28-wide steel tray beside the axis. The tray hangs flush under the plate, clear of the box screws, so the axis is free from floor to plate (45.4) for the cord, a strain relief and two Class 2 splices. The canopy stays 150 x 50 with the cord centered, nothing visible changes, the CAD finds 0 clashes against today's parts, and the cost is about the same as O1.
O1 is then unnecessary: it moves the cord 20 off center for nothing. O2 is also unnecessary, and its +12 is probably too much: Heyco's 11.1 body length includes a head of about 4.7 that stays outside, so +4 to +8 would do.
Runner-up: the strain relief in the canopy's floor with the driver flat (150 x 50, about 3 mm margin, a visible black head). I found no slimmer listed phase-cut driver for this load, and a remote driver suits a bar fit-out only.

findings.claim:
The lane stopped because 'the cord can't stay centered in 150 x 50'. It can. Stand the same ERP driver on edge in a narrow tray beside the axis (frame: x on the cables' line; heights above the canopy's underside).
- Tray: 1.0 steel, x -35 to -7, y -56 to +39, z 6.4 to 48.4. Its top is open and the plate closes it. It hangs on two PEM FH-M3-8 studs through two tabs: one off the outer wall at y -52 to -40, one off the inner end.
- Driver: on edge at x -34 to -8.8, y -53 to +31, z 7.9 to 47.9. Its two tabs are screwed to the tray's outer wall.
- Input leads (300 mm, -XL): they rise in the tray's 7 mm inner end gap and go straight up through a rolled Ø7 hole in the plate at (-21, 34.5) into the 4 in box, where they are spliced. There is no 120 V wiring in the canopy at all.
